data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Xanthomas** (Nutritional & metabolic)_

**Q1. What are xanthomas?**
- Yellowish papules, plaques, nodules or tendon swellings formed by lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in skin/tendons — often markers of hyperlipidaemia (primary or secondary) but can occur with normal lipids (normolipaemic)

**Q2. Describe the clinical types and lipid associations.**
- Eruptive xanthomas: crops of small red-yellow papules with erythematous halo on buttocks, extensors — high triglycerides (types I, IV, V; uncontrolled diabetes) — risk of acute pancreatitis
- Tuberous xanthomas: firm yellow nodules on elbows, knees, buttocks — types II, III (dysbetalipoproteinaemia)
- Tendinous xanthomas: smooth nodules in Achilles tendon, extensor tendons of hands — type IIa familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor defect), also cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, sitosterolaemia
- Planar: xanthelasma palpebrarum (eyelids — commonest; ~50% have normal lipids), palmar crease xanthomas (xanthoma striatum palmare — type III dysbetalipoproteinaemia, pathognomonic), intertriginous (finger webs — homozygous FH), diffuse plane xanthomas (normolipaemic — paraproteinaemia/myeloma)
- Verruciform xanthoma (oral/genital), xanthoma disseminatum (non-LCH histiocytosis, normolipaemic, with diabetes insipidus)

**Q3. Classify primary hyperlipoproteinaemia (Fredrickson — PYQ).**
- Type I: raised chylomicrons (lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II deficiency) — eruptive xanthomas, lipaemia retinalis, pancreatitis, hepatosplenomegaly; childhood
- Type IIa: raised LDL (familial hypercholesterolaemia — LDLR, APOB, PCSK9) — tendon, tuberous xanthomas, xanthelasma, arcus, premature CAD
- Type IIb: raised LDL + VLDL (familial combined) — xanthelasma, tuberous
- Type III: raised IDL/chylomicron remnants (dysbetalipoproteinaemia — apo E2/E2) — palmar crease and tubero-eruptive xanthomas
- Type IV: raised VLDL (familial hypertriglyceridaemia) — eruptive xanthomas; associated diabetes, obesity
- Type V: raised VLDL + chylomicrons — eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis

**Q4. Secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia.**
- Diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, chronic kidney disease, cholestasis (primary biliary cholangitis — planar xanthomas), obesity, alcohol, pancreatitis
- Drugs: oral retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin), oestrogens, corticosteroids, cyclosporine, protease inhibitors, β-blockers, thiazides, olanzapine

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Dermal collections of foam cells (macrophages with lipid vacuoles), Touton giant cells (wreath of nuclei), extracellular cholesterol clefts (tuberous/tendinous), inflammation in eruptive xanthomas
- Lipids dissolved during processing — frozen section + Oil Red O / Sudan stains show lipid

**Q6. Investigations.**
- Fasting lipid profile (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides), lipoprotein electrophoresis, apo E genotype (type III)
- Blood sugar/HbA1c, thyroid function, renal function, urine protein, LFT
- Serum protein electrophoresis/immunofixation for plane xanthomas with normal lipids
- Cardiovascular risk assessment (ECG, lipid targets); family screening for FH

**Q7. Write short notes on Tangier's disease (PYQ).**
- Autosomal recessive ABCA1 deficiency → almost absent HDL; cholesterol esters accumulate in reticuloendothelial tissues — enlarged orange-yellow tonsils (pathognomonic), hepatosplenomegaly, peripheral neuropathy, premature atherosclerosis, corneal clouding

**Q8. Treatment of xanthomas.**
- Treat underlying lipid disorder: diet, weight loss, exercise, glycaemic control, treat hypothyroidism; statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors (FH), fibrates/omega-3 for hypertriglyceridaemia — eruptive xanthomas regress in weeks with TG control
- Local for xanthelasma/persistent lesions: TCA 50–70% application, surgical excision, CO2/Er:YAG/Q-switched/fractional lasers, radiofrequency, cryotherapy, intralesional pingyangmycin/bleomycin
- Tendon xanthomas regress slowly with aggressive lipid lowering; surgery only if functional problems

**Q9. Significance of xanthelasma.**
- Commonest xanthoma; ~50% normolipaemic but independently linked with myocardial infarction and atherosclerosis risk (Copenhagen study) — always check lipids and CV risk

## Quick spotter facts
- Crops of yellow papules with red halo on buttocks — eruptive xanthomas (high TG → pancreatitis risk)
- Palmar crease xanthomas — type III
- Achilles tendon xanthoma — familial hypercholesterolaemia

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Xanthomas and lipid disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
